mean: used to say clearly that this is your opinion
ex: In my view, the school should teach first aid before it teaches another chapter of trigonometry.
note: Put it at the start with a comma. Don't stack it: 'In my view, I think' says the same thing twice.
ex2: In my view, Ravi bats better at number four than as an opener, whatever the selectors say.

mean: used before saying what you really think, even if it is unwelcome
ex: To be honest, I found the wedding food too oily, but I didn't say so to Aunty.
note: Overuse makes people wonder whether your other sentences were dishonest. Save it for a truly difficult opinion.
ex2: To be honest, the startup's pitch was exciting, but the numbers did not add up for me.

mean: a way of looking at something, shaped by who you are
ex: From a farmer's point of view, a late monsoon is not just news; it is a whole year's income at risk.
note: Say 'from my point of view', not 'according to my point of view'.
ex2: Try to see the umpire's point of view: he had one second to decide and no replay.

mean: what you think or believe about something
ex: In the family WhatsApp group, everyone had an opinion on Kiran's choice of college.
note: Say 'in my opinion', not 'according to my opinion'. An opinion is not a fact, so back it with a reason.
ex2: Before the knee surgery, Mr Bose asked for a second opinion from a doctor in Vellore.

mean: used to give an example that supports what you just said
ex: Small habits matter; for instance, one cloth bag saves the vegetable seller dozens of plastic bags a month.
note: Same as 'for example'. Put commas around it: 'Some cities, for instance Indore, have become much cleaner.'
ex2: Our coach changes small things; for instance, we now warm up with football before every cricket session.

mean: your personal opinion or way of understanding something
ex: What's your take on the new rule that everyone must come to the Bengaluru office three days a week?
note: Informal and very common: 'My take on it is...'. Use 'view' in formal writing.
ex2: Aditi's take on the film was that the songs were great but the second half dragged.

mean: said honestly and directly, even if it is not pleasant
ex: Frankly, Sameer, the business plan needs real numbers before we show it to your uncle in Surat.
note: 'Frankly speaking' is common in India, but 'frankly' alone is enough and sounds sharper.
ex2: Frankly, the hostel mess food has got worse this month, and the students deserve an explanation.

mean: to think carefully about the good and bad sides before deciding
ex: Before accepting the Dubai job, Shalini sat down to weigh up the salary against time away from her parents.
with: weigh up the pros and cons
note: British English says 'weigh up'; American English often just 'weigh'. It needs an object: 'weigh up the costs'.
ex2: Farmers in Punjab weigh up the cost of seeds and water before choosing between rice and maize.

mean: a sensible remark you accept, even if you still disagree overall
ex: Mira raised a fair point: if the meeting has no agenda, why are ten people sitting in it?
note: A gracious way to accept part of an argument. It shows you listen, which makes your own view land better.
ex2: Dad grumbled, but admitted his son had made a fair point about reading reviews before buying the car.

mean: used to give your opinion, based on your own position or experience
ex: From where I stand, as a nurse on night duty, the new shift timings are simply unsafe.
note: It admits that your view comes from your own place, so it sounds fair, not arrogant. Change 'I' to fit the speaker.
ex2: From where I stand, behind the counter of this chai stall, the whole street's mood changes when it rains.

mean: used to show that this is your own view, not everyone's
ex: Personally, I prefer the slow toy train to Ooty; the view is worth the extra hours.
note: Avoid 'personally I myself feel': one word is enough. It also means 'in person': 'she thanked him personally'.
ex2: Personally, I would wait for the official results before celebrating, but the whole colony is already bursting crackers.

mean: the position or set of ideas from which you judge something
ex: From a safety standpoint, the old bridge over the river should be closed until it is repaired.
note: More formal than 'point of view'. A common pattern: 'from a legal, financial or safety standpoint'.
ex2: From a teacher's standpoint, online classes saved travel time but made it hard to see who was lost.

mean: a strong belief that you hold firmly
ex: Nirmala spoke with such conviction about clean drinking water that the gram sabha agreed to fix the handpump.
note: It also means being found guilty in court. 'Speak with conviction' means sounding sure because you truly believe it.
ex2: The young debater lost the round but won the room, because she argued with real conviction.

mean: the most important part of a problem or argument
ex: The crux of the matter is simple: the flat has no parking, and Raghav owns two cars.
note: Usually 'the crux of the matter, problem or issue'. Naming it helps you cut through side points in a discussion.
ex2: After an hour of debate, the moderator said the crux was whether the city needs more buses or wider roads.

mean: in a very direct way, without trying to soften it
ex: Put bluntly, the Indiranagar café will close in six months unless we cut costs now.
note: Blunt can sound rude. 'To put it bluntly' warns the listener that a hard truth is coming.
ex2: The coach told the team bluntly that nobody's place in the state squad was safe after that loss.

mean: after thinking about all the points for and against
ex: On balance, renting near the Whitefield office makes more sense than buying a flat an hour away.
note: Shows you have weighed both sides, so your opinion sounds fair. It usually comes first, followed by a comma.
ex2: On balance, the doctors felt a small operation was safer than months of strong painkillers.

mean: in very few words, giving only the main point
ex: In a nutshell, the new scheme means fewer forms for small shopkeepers and faster refunds.
note: Useful at the end of a long explanation. Keep the 'a': not 'in nutshell'.
ex2: In a nutshell, Nanu's advice on marriage was this: listen more, and never go to bed angry.

mean: used to offer your opinion modestly, not knowing if it will help
ex: For what it's worth, Ananya, I think the Pune college has better teachers than the famous one in Delhi.
note: A humble way to share a view without pushing it. Don't overuse it in meetings, or you will sound unsure.
ex2: For what it's worth, the old mechanic said the scooter only needed a new spark plug, not a new engine.

mean: to give reasons that show why something is right or needed
ex: Rohan used two years of electricity bills to make the case for solar panels on the society's roof.
note: 'Make the case for X' or 'make the case that...'. A strong case uses facts and examples, not volume.
ex2: At the hostel meeting, Zoya tried to make the case for keeping the library open till midnight during exams.

mean: most important or most noticeable
ex: In two minutes, the lawyer listed the salient points of the land dispute for the judge.
note: Common in Indian textbooks as 'salient features'. In speech, 'key points' often sounds more natural.
ex2: The salient fact about the new phone is simple: the battery lasts two full days.

mean: saying clearly and honestly what you think
ex: The forthright nurse told the family exactly what the recovery would involve, without false hope.
note: Usually praise: honest and direct but not rude. Blunt can be rude; forthright rarely is.
ex2: Mrs Fernandes was forthright at the parent-teacher meeting: too much tuition was tiring the children out.

mean: having strong opinions and pushing them without listening to others
ex: My opinionated uncle can turn any family dinner into a lecture on how the cricket team should be picked.
instead: always has to have his say
note: This is criticism. Having views is good; being opinionated means not listening. Aim to be clear, not opinionated.
ex2: The food blogger is opinionated about everything, but her Kolkata street-food reviews are honest and useful.

mean: sharp, clear and forceful in criticism or argument
ex: The editor's trenchant column on potholes pushed the city to repair the main road before the monsoon.
note: A strong, formal word for writing and reviews. Trenchant criticism cuts deep but is based on reasons.
ex2: Her trenchant review of the over-hyped film was shared thousands of times on social media.

mean: a set of beliefs that guides how someone lives or works
ex: Uncle Thomas's credo for his bakery was simple: fresh bread daily, honest prices, and no credit.
note: A rare, formal word from the Latin for 'I believe'. In speech, 'motto' or 'principle' is more common.
ex2: The coach's credo, 'fitness first, talent second', is painted on the wall of the Jalandhar hockey academy.
